newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Republic truce holds.
newsitem.headline: Central African Republic truce holds.

text.p: Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic, remained calm on Sunday and a four-day truce in fighting between disaffected soldiers and African peacemakers appeared to be holding.
Residents said there had been no new clashes since the truce came into effect at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Saturday.
However, the mutineers had still made no move to hand over their heavy weapons, as required under the truce, brokered by Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure.

French ambassador Jean-Marc Simon told RFI radio that "the restitution of the heavy arms is essential, of paramount importance for any solution to the crisis that is going to lead finally to a definitive ceasefire".

Under the deal, the dissident soldiers, a minority of whom never rejoined their units despite a January deal that ended a previous mutiny, are supposed to hand their mortars and other heavy weapons over to the French ambassador.
A few mortars were handed over in a symbolic ceremony on Friday, but no more weapons have been forthcoming since.
The Central African Red Cross says about 100 people, mostly civilians caught in crossfire, have been killed in the fighting and at least 150 wounded.
France has given the Red Cross 27 million CFA francs ($47,000) to provide emergency help to people displaced by the fighting.
The U.N. refugee has estimated that 60,000 people fled into the countryside to escape the fighting in the capital, and it has appealed for tents to provide them with shelter.

Residents said a few people had ventured back to their homes in the southern districts of the capital, close to the mutineers' stronghold at the Camp Kassai barracks, but most had decided to stay in the north and the surrounding countryside.
The latest battles were sparked by an incident between some of the former mutineers and African peacekeepers on June 20.

Talks were expected to continue on Monday on ways to relaunch the January deal, which was signed by President Ange-Felix Patasse, the mutineers and representatives of all political groups and society at large.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as pay protests but evolved into a bid to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north, elected in 1993. A third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.

Former colonial power France, which has troops in the country under a defence pact, intervened in support of the peacekeepers and one of its helicopters hit mortar batteries manned by dissident soldiers after its embassy came under fire.
